newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives part ways over Europe.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives part ways over Europe.

text.p: Britain's ruling party was at war over plans for a single European currency on Sunday after a top minister said Conservative candidates should contest the May 1 election on whatever line suited them.

Defence Minister Michael Portillo, a prominent Euro-sceptic who is believed to have designs on the party leadership, said it was "perfectly reasonable" for candidates to stray from the official party line on Europe.

"The Labour Party has sought to produce a situation where all MPs are merely automata, who are programmed...and sent off to say exactly the same thing in the same moment at the same place," said Portillo. "That isn't real democracy."
Labour -- which has its own rifts over Europe -- crowed over the split, saying a clear majority of Conservative candidates it surveyed were flouting the party's official policy.
Prime Minister John Major has adopted a wait-and-see line, saying he will decide nearer the time if it makes sense to join and only after he has consulted the British people.

Conservative strategists had hoped that such a carefully honed line -- critics called it fudged -- would paper over internal party differences over how closely Britain should link its economic destiny with that of the continent.
Labour said the rift was now plain for all to see.

"The Tory truce on the single currency has collapsed. Tory MPs are not observing a ceasefire but are using their election literature to fire a shot across the bows of John Major," said foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook. "Britain cannot afford to have a government rent by such division and chaos.
Cook said 55 of the first 100 election addresses to be published by Conservative candidates had declared their opposition to a single currency.
"John Major is in danger of becoming John Minor within his own party," he said.
Major has gradually shifted towards the Euro-sceptic wing of his party, whose cause has been championed by such Conservative grandees as former prime minister Margaret Thatcher.
On Sunday, Major insisted the real split was not in his own party but between the Conservatives and the opposition parties, which could not be trusted to fight for Britain in Europe.

"There is one clear, distinct divide," he told Sky News television. "They're essentially federalist. They will go down the route towards a centralist Europe. We will not. That is the very clear divide between the parties and upon this issue I have absolutely no doubt that we are marching with the general direction, drift and instincts of the British nation."
Europe sprung back onto the election agenda last week when a junior farming minister went her own way on the single currency -- and won Major's backing in the process.

Yet the decision by so many Conservatives to defy Major on the single currency -- among the most important issues facing Britain in the next decade -- only serves to underline opposition taunts of weak leadership in the ruling party.

A millionaire businessman has already offered campaign funds to Conservative candidates who oppose a single currency, and says he expects the offer to be taken up by around 200 -- almost a third of all Conservative candidates.
Sir James Goldsmith's Referendum Party held a rally in London on Sunday to push its anti-Brussels message.
The tycoon has impressed Euro-sceptics with his tough line and one disaffected Conservative even defected to his cause last month, giving the Referendum Party its first seat in parliament.
